matching_records.english_copy: The Collect gathers the prayer of the Church for the particular Mass and commonly concludes through Christ in a formal liturgical ending. Its text varies with the day or formulary.
In the 1962 Mass the Gradual belongs to the chants between the readings. Its use and what follows it depend on the liturgical day and season.
In the 1962 Roman Missal the Tract is especially associated with penitential periods and particular Masses. It is a liturgical chant with its own appointed text, not simply any long psalm.
The Offertory antiphon is distinct from the priest’s offertory prayers and from the broader theological act of offering. Its text varies with the Mass formulary.
The Preface begins after the dialogue Sursum corda and Gratias agamus Domino Deo nostro. Different prefaces are appointed according to season, feast or Mass.
The Communion antiphon belongs to the Proper and varies with the formulary. It should not be confused with the sacramental act of Holy Communion, even though both use the word Communio.
The Postcommunion asks for the fruits of the sacrament or other graces appropriate to the celebration. Its text varies with the Mass and follows the Communion rites according to the rubrics.
A profound bow is more substantial than a simple bow of the head. It is a technical ceremonial action in the traditional Mass and should be linked to the exact cue rather than approximated visually.
The crucifer’s place and movements depend on the procession and ceremonial. The role is functional and may be fulfilled by different classes of server according to local and ritual practice.
The Master of Ceremonies ensures that ministers, books, objects and movements follow the rubrics. The role is practical and ceremonial and does not itself confer sacramental authority.
The exact scope of ‘sacred ministers’ depends on historical and ritual context. In the 1962 Solemn Mass it commonly denotes the deacon and subdeacon assisting the priest celebrant.
The processional cross is a movable liturgical object and should be distinguished from a fixed altar crucifix or rood. Its place in the procession depends on the rite.
A procession is an action, not merely a calendar label. Ad Orientem therefore requires evidence that a procession actually occurs rather than inferring one from the feast alone.
The exact entrance order varies by the form of Mass, ministers present and local ceremonial. It is distinct from devotional processions such as Corpus Christi or Rogations.
The term can refer to the chant or, by extension, the entire sprinkling rite. During Paschaltide the corresponding antiphon is Vidi aquam.
The cantor can begin chants, sing solo verses or lead the schola according to the rite. The role should be distinguished from the broader choir or schola as a collective body.
In the Mass, chants such as the Introit, Offertory and Communion preserve antiphonal origins or form. ‘Antiphon’ should not be used as a generic synonym for every chant.
In psalmody, intonation is one component of the tone before the reciting pitch. In ceremonial usage, a cantor or celebrant may intone a chant before the schola or others continue it.
In liturgical books an incipit can function as a title-like identifier for a prayer or chant. In music it can also mean the portion intoned before others continue.
The response is commonly marked ℟. or R. and belongs to the dialogical structure of the rite. It is not synonymous with responsory, which is a more developed chant form.
The Kyrie retains Greek in the Latin Roman rite and is arranged according to the form of Mass and chant. It is an invocation for mercy, not simply an introductory song title.
The Gloria is not used at every Mass. In the 1962 Missal its presence depends on the liturgical class, season and type of Mass according to the rubrics.
The Sanctus joins biblical acclamations of divine holiness and forms part of the fixed Ordinary. In sung Mass it belongs to the schola’s Ordinary repertoire.
In traditional sung practice the Benedictus can be musically separated from the Sanctus around the Canon, although textually they form one liturgical unit.
Low Mass (Missa lecta) is a liturgical mode of celebration, not a judgment about solemnity or spiritual value. Its texts are spoken rather than rendered according to the sung ceremonial.
Solemn Mass (Missa solemnis) is defined by its ministers and ceremonial structure, not simply by the importance of the feast or the amount of music used.
Roman ceremonial distinguishes different degrees of bow. The exact form and occasion must be taken from the relevant rubric rather than inferred from the generic word bow.
Standing can signify readiness, honour and common prayer. As with kneeling, its exact use is governed by the liturgical profile and rubrics rather than by a timeless posture chart.
Sitting is a legitimate liturgical posture whose occasions depend on the rite and role. A congregation’s local custom can differ from the ceremonial directions applying to clergy or ministers.
The historical minor order and the current instituted ministry of acolyte are related but not identical juridical forms. The glossary therefore treats acolyte as a multi-layer term.
Torchbearers are especially associated with the Canon, elevations and Communion in traditional ceremonial. Their number and exact movements depend on the form of Mass and local ceremonial practice.
‘Celebrant’ describes a liturgical role in a given function. It does not by itself identify canonical office, jurisdiction, community affiliation or personal status.
Incense is used according to the rite at altars, Gospel, offerings, Blessed Sacrament, clergy and faithful. Its use is liturgical and symbolic, not magical.
Vidi aquam is not an interchangeable stylistic alternative to Asperges me; the liturgical season determines which antiphon is appointed.
Blessings belong to the Church’s sacramental life but are not all sacraments. Their minister, formula and effects depend on the liturgical book and law governing the particular blessing.
Liturgical kisses are technical gestures whose object and timing matter. They should not be interpreted through modern social conventions but according to the rite’s ceremonial meaning.
St Pius X gave Gregorian chant a normative place in Roman sacred music. The term refers to a real musical repertory and style, not merely any unaccompanied Latin singing.
Plainchant is broader than Gregorian chant. Not every form of plainchant belongs to the Gregorian repertory, though Gregorian chant is the principal Roman example.
The communion rail has both architectural and liturgical functions in many traditional churches. Its presence is not itself a sacramental requirement, and local arrangements can differ.
The chalice is a principal sacred vessel and is reserved for Eucharistic use according to liturgical law. Its ceremonial preparation and purification are governed by the rite being celebrated.
The alb is common to several ordained and instituted ministries in Latin liturgical tradition. It should be distinguished from the shorter surplice and from prelatial garments such as the rochet.
The dalmatic is distinct from the priest’s chasuble and the subdeacon’s tunicle. In traditional Roman ceremonial its use identifies the deacon’s liturgical role within the solemn ministry.
The cope is not a Mass vestment in the strict sense and is used in a wide range of non-Eucharistic or processional rites. Its use depends on the ceremony and the minister.
The humeral veil is especially associated with Benediction and Eucharistic processions, but it also appears in other ceremonial contexts. Its colour and use depend on the rite.
The cincture secures the alb and belongs to traditional liturgical vesture. Its use is practical and symbolic, but the precise vesting customs vary by rite and period.
The biretta is a traditional clerical and ceremonial article whose colour and entitlement vary with rank and usage. It is not an essential vestment for the validity of any sacrament.
The rochet resembles a shortened alb but is a prelatial choir garment, not a substitute for the alb at Mass. Its use is governed by rank and ceremonial law.
The zucchetto or solideo is clerical dress rather than a sacramental vestment. Its use and colour are determined by ecclesiastical custom and office.
The manuterge is a practical liturgical linen associated with the washing of hands. It is distinct from the purificator, which is used with the chalice and other sacred vessels.
The sanctuary lamp signals Eucharistic reservation and expresses honour to the Blessed Sacrament. Its form and fuel can vary according to law and legitimate custom.
A reliquary protects relics and presents them for lawful veneration. The object itself is not the relic and should not be confused with a tabernacle or pyx used for the Blessed Sacrament.
The narthex has varied architectural and liturgical functions across periods. It is an architectural term and should not be treated as a universal requirement of every church building.
A high altar is distinguished from side altars and secondary altars. The term describes architectural and liturgical prominence, not a doctrinally superior kind of altar.
The pulpit is primarily architectural and homiletic. It differs from the liturgical ambo, although in some churches a single structure may have served overlapping functions.
The ambo has ancient roots and a specific liturgical function. It should not automatically be equated with every pulpit or portable lectern.
The baptismal font is a sacramental furnishing and can be located in a baptistery, chapel or church area according to architecture and law. It is distinct from a holy-water stoup.
The stoup supports devotional use of holy water, especially the Sign of the Cross on entering or leaving. It must be distinguished from the baptismal font, which serves the sacrament of Baptism.
Sacred vestments have distinct names, users and ceremonial meanings. The traditional Roman Mass uses a specific vesture system whose individual items are separately defined in the glossary.
The sacristy is a functional sacred-service space rather than the sanctuary itself. Many ceremonial actions begin or end there, but its arrangement varies considerably among churches.
The purificator is a functional sacred linen used especially around Communion and purification. It should not be confused with the corporal, which is spread on the altar beneath the sacred vessels.
The thurible is carried and handled by the thurifer according to detailed ceremonial rules. It is distinct from the incense boat, which holds the incense before it is placed on the coals.
The incense boat, traditionally often boat-shaped, normally accompanies the thurible and includes or is used with a spoon for placing incense on the coals.
The aspergillum is the implement; aspersion is the action performed with it. Traditional forms vary, including brush-like or perforated forms designed to retain and scatter blessed water.
The surplice is shorter and differently cut from the alb. It is common in choir, serving, blessings and other rites, but it does not replace the alb where the rubrics require the latter.
Cassock colour and trimming can indicate rank or institute, but the basic garment is not itself a sacramental vestment. Particular law and custom govern current clerical dress.
The chalice veil belongs to the traditional arrangement of chalice, paten, pall, corporal and burse. It is distinct from the humeral veil and ciborium veil.
The altar stone belongs especially to older Latin discipline and portable-altars practice. It should not be presented as a current universal requirement for every altar.
The nave is distinguished from the sanctuary, choir and side chapels. Historical church plans can use the term with architectural nuances, but it broadly denotes the main congregational space.
Side altars historically supported additional Masses and particular devotions. Their presence and use vary with church architecture and liturgical discipline.
The cathedral takes its name from the cathedra. It must be distinguished from ordinary sedilia or celebrant seating, which do not signify diocesan episcopal authority.
The medieval and early modern jubé took many forms and functions. It is a historical architectural feature, not a universal requirement of traditional Catholic churches.
The grille protects anonymity and remains explicitly provided for in current canon law. Its availability does not prevent other lawful forms of confession where the law permits them.
Retables range from simple painted panels to monumental architectural compositions. They are devotional-architectural furnishings, not part of the altar’s sacramental essence.

The altar is distinct from the tabernacle even when the tabernacle stands upon or behind it. Its consecration or blessing, relics and construction are governed by liturgical and canonical norms that differ across historical periods.

The tabernacle is the place of Eucharistic reservation and therefore a focal point of adoration when the Blessed Sacrament is present. It is not synonymous with altar, sanctuary or architectural ciborium.

The paten is paired ceremonially with the chalice in the Roman Mass. Its exact form and use vary by period and rite, but it is distinct from the ciborium used for reserving or distributing multiple Hosts.
In Catholic liturgical Latin anima commonly refers to the human soul, as in prayers for the dead or Communion formulas. Biblical usage can be broader, so lexical context matters.
The plural caeli is common in liturgical phrases such as Pleni sunt caeli et terra. Translation depends on whether the text speaks cosmologically, poetically or theologically.
In saecula saeculorum is an idiomatic biblical-liturgical formula meaning ‘for ever and ever’. Learners should not translate it mechanically as ‘into the centuries of centuries’.
The verb is central to liturgical prayer and underlies Oremus, ‘Let us pray’. Its exact English or French rendering depends on whether the context stresses prayer, petition or address.
The verb appears in praise of God and in biblical-liturgical language of manifesting glory. It is a regular first-conjugation ecclesiastical Latin verb.
N. stands for nomen, ‘name’. The specific person or saint intended must be supplied from the liturgical context rather than pronounced as the letter itself.
Sedet is the present form of sedeo. The subject is determined by the ceremonial context, usually the celebrant or another minister.
Secreto is a technical voice-direction term in the traditional Mass. It does not mean the prayer is esoteric or hidden from doctrine; it describes how it is recited.
Submissa voce identifies a quieter vocal level in traditional rubrical language. It should be mapped consistently to the app’s priest-voice state rather than translated differently card by card.
The ablative construction describes the celebrant’s action of raising the eyes at specified moments. It should link directly to the visual/action cue rather than remain as untranslated rubric text.
The adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case. In titles such as Sanctus Spiritus or Sancta Maria the translation depends on the noun and established devotional usage.
Liturgical translation varies with context: beata Maria is conventionally ‘Blessed Mary’, while a generic biblical sentence may use ‘blessed’ or ‘happy’.
The noun is frequent in collects, psalms and penitential prayer. It can denote God’s merciful disposition or acts of mercy according to context.
Gloria can denote divine glory, honour or praise and appears in fixed liturgical texts such as Gloria Patri and Gloria in excelsis Deo. The lexeme should link to those phrases.
Pax is a third-declension noun, genitive pacis, frequent in blessings and Mass texts such as Pax Domini sit semper vobiscum. Its theological sense is determined by the phrase context.
Corpus is a third-declension neuter noun, genitive corporis, central to Eucharistic phrases such as Corpus Christi and Hoc est enim Corpus meum.
Sanguis is a third-declension noun, genitive sanguinis, frequent in Eucharistic and biblical texts. Liturgical capitalization does not change its morphology.
The same lexeme can denote the Church as the ecclesial body or a local church/building depending on context. The lexeme therefore links to several concepts rather than forcing one definition.
Terra is a regular first-declension noun and appears constantly in biblical and liturgical contrasts with caelum.
Oremus is the first-person plural present subjunctive of oro used hortatorily. It functions as a fixed liturgical cue and therefore belongs primarily to the phrase layer.
Quaeso is defective in classical usage and quaesumus survives frequently as a conventional liturgical petition formula. Its idiomatic translation is more natural than a mechanical grammatical gloss.
Concede is a standard liturgical petition verb. It is usually best translated idiomatically as ‘grant’ rather than with the modern sense of reluctantly conceding an argument.
Miserere is the imperative of the deponent verb misereor and governs the genitive in classical-liturgical usage, as in miserere nobis.
Benedico is formed from bene and dico and in liturgical usage denotes blessing or speaking blessing. It gives rise to forms such as benedicimus and benedictus.
In Christian Latin the verb often carries the theological sense of hope in God or His promises, but grammar and context determine the exact object.
Diligere and amare overlap but are not always interchangeable in nuance. Scriptural and liturgical Latin frequently uses diligo for love of God and neighbour.
Suscipio has a wide range of liturgical uses, from receiving gifts or persons to taking something up. Translation should be phrase-specific.
The irregular compound of fero is central to offertory and sacrificial language. Its forms should be taught as a lexical family rather than inferred from a regular conjugation.
The verb appears especially in prayers for the dead and gives the vocabulary behind requiem, ‘rest’. Its theological sense comes from the prayer context, not from the verb alone.
Dignus often governs an ablative or appears in fixed liturgical formulas such as Dignum et iustum est and Domine, non sum dignus.
The phrase is a Christological conclusion used in collects and other prayers, with grammatical variations depending on whether Christ, the Father and the Holy Ghost have been named in the prayer.
Dicitur is the passive form of dico and directs that the specified text be said. The grammatical form is useful for learners because rubrics frequently use impersonal or passive constructions.
In the 1962 calendar ferias have classes and can enjoy differing precedence according to season and day. Feria therefore does not mean an empty date with no liturgical identity.
In the 1962 system a commemoration can affect collects and other appointed elements without replacing the principal Mass. Its availability and number are strictly controlled by the precedence rules.
In the 1962 profile Eastertide has its own calendar and chant characteristics. Its exact boundaries and octave structures belong to the governing rubrics rather than to a generic modern season label.
The 1962 rubrics classify votive Masses and regulate when they may replace the day’s Mass. Personal preference alone does not override the liturgical calendar.
A funeral Mass is one particular class or occasion of Mass for the Dead and should not be treated as synonymous with every Requiem or anniversary Mass.
The universal calendar provides the common Roman framework but does not exhaust every celebration observed locally. Particular calendars add legitimately proper feasts and observances.
First-class days enjoy the strongest precedence under the 1962 rubrics. The classification must not be confused with the older double/semidouble system abolished before the 1962 Missal.
Second-class days have defined precedence and liturgical privileges below first-class days but above third- and fourth-class days.
Fourth-class days have the least precedence in the 1962 system but still possess real liturgical identity. They are not equivalent to an absence of observance.
Requiem Masses have distinctive texts and omissions, including changes to the Ordinary. Their classes and permitted occasions are governed separately by the 1962 rubrics.
Certain ferias, especially in major penitential seasons, can outrank feasts or restrict commemorations. The exact privileges depend on the 1962 table and rubric.
‘Feast’ is a broad liturgical term whose rank depends on the calendar system in force. Historical labels such as double or semidouble must not be mixed with the 1962 class system.
Sundays possess their own rank and precedence according to season in the Roman calendar. Their liturgical observance is related to, but distinct from, the canonical obligation to attend Mass.
Double belonged to the older classification system and included further grades such as greater doubles and doubles of different classes. It is historical terminology and not a 1962 rank.
Semidouble was abolished as an operative rank before the 1962 Missal. When encountered in older missals or manuals it must be displayed as historical terminology.

A liturgical vigil is a technical calendar category and should not be confused automatically with any evening prayer service or with the modern notion that every feast begins with an anticipated evening Mass.
Advent combines expectation, preparation and penitential restraint without being identical in discipline to Lent. Its Sundays and ferias form part of the Temporal cycle.

In the traditional Roman calendar Lent has its own ferial Masses, ceremonial characteristics and progression toward Passiontide and Holy Week. Liturgical identity and current fasting law are related but distinct layers.

The 1962 Roman books distinguish the Greater Litany and the Minor Litanies or Rogations. Their calendar occurrence does not by itself prove that a procession actually takes place; the app therefore requires an explicit following-action or local witness.
Third-class days include many feasts and ferias and are governed by the precedence rules of the 1960 reform. Their treatment cannot be inferred from pre-1960 rank names.
This is the broader category under which funeral, anniversary and other permitted Requiem Masses fall. Exact terminology and rank are determined by the rubrics.
Occurrence is resolved by the table of precedence and rules governing omission, commemoration or transfer. It concerns same-day competition and must be distinguished from concurrence.
Concurrence is principally an Office concept and is distinct from occurrence, which concerns celebrations falling on the same calendar day.
Transfer is not a discretionary rescheduling. It occurs only when the rubrics or competent authority provide for it after a higher-ranking observance takes precedence.
Commons include categories such as apostles, martyrs, confessors and virgins. A saint’s proper texts can be combined with a Common according to the Missal.
The monstrance or ostensorium normally holds the Host in a lunette. It is a Eucharistic vessel and must not be confused with a reliquary, though historical forms can resemble one another.
The lunette is inserted into the monstrance for exposition and removed according to the rites of reservation. It is a sacred Eucharistic accessory, not an independent devotional object.
The visit can include silent adoration, acts of faith, reparation, thanksgiving and spiritual communion. It is devotional rather than a separate sacrament or liturgical office.
The text comes from Saint Thomas Aquinas’s hymn Verbum supernum prodiens. In practice it functions as a prayer text and Latin phrase object linked to Eucharistic adoration.
The Divine Praises form an approved devotional text associated with Eucharistic worship. Their individual invocations should remain textually stable and source-backed.
The pyx is smaller and more portable than a ciborium and is used according to the rites governing Eucharistic transport and Communion outside Mass.
The ciborium veil marks the sacred vessel used for Eucharistic reservation. It must be distinguished from the chalice veil and humeral veil.
Exposition is governed by liturgical law concerning minister, place, vessel, candles, incense and prayer. It is distinct from simple reservation in the tabernacle.
Reposition concludes a period of exposition. It should be distinguished from Benediction, since exposition can end by reposition without the blessing with the Blessed Sacrament in some circumstances.
The Forty Hours devotion combines prolonged adoration with a defined ceremonial tradition. Historical rules and indulgences attached to it must not be assumed unchanged in current law.
The phrase means ‘Thou gavest them bread from heaven’ and is answered according to the rite before the concluding prayer. It belongs primarily to the Latin phrase layer.
‘Blessed Sacrament’ is a devotional and liturgical title for the Eucharist. It refers to Christ sacramentally present and should not be confused with a generic blessed object or sacramental.
Reservation serves especially Communion of the sick and Eucharistic worship. The place, vessel and conditions of reservation are governed by liturgical and canonical law.
Pious exercises should harmonize with and lead toward the liturgy rather than replace it. Their authority and obligation differ from sacramental and liturgical law.
The word ‘act’ in devotional collections refers to a prayer that expresses and elicits the named disposition. It does not mean that reciting the words mechanically guarantees the interior act.
Devotional consecration is not the same as Eucharistic consecration or canonical religious profession. The term expresses dedication and belonging in a devotional sense.

A novena is a devotional form, not a sacrament or universal liturgical obligation. Particular novenas have their own history, texts and recommended start dates; current indulgences must be verified separately from historical grants.

The exposition throne belongs to traditional ceremonial arrangements for public Eucharistic worship. It is not required in every form of exposition and should be presented as a ceremonial furnishing, not a doctrinal necessity.
Aspirations or ejaculatory prayers help maintain recollection and frequent turning of the heart to God. They can be spontaneous or drawn from approved prayers and Scripture.
Mental prayer includes meditation and more simple affective forms. It is not opposed to vocal prayer, since vocal prayer can also be attentive and interior.
Catholic meditation is ordered toward conversion and union with God rather than mere analysis. Methods can help, but the method is a means rather than the substance of prayer.
Spiritual reading is not mere information gathering. It is undertaken slowly and reflectively so that truth can shape prayer and conduct.
An examination of conscience should be truthful and proportionate rather than scrupulous. It seeks concrete moral responsibility, not an endless search for absolute psychological certainty.

The component practices, timing and intention should be stated from reliable Fatima sources. It is a private-devotional practice approved and promoted by the Church, not a new sacrament or universal precept.

Litanies can be liturgical or devotional depending on the text and context. Approved litanies have defined texts; the word should not be used as though any list of petitions were automatically an official litany.
The episcopate is the fullness of Holy Orders. Context determines whether the term refers sacramentally to the degree of order or collectively to bishops as a body.
The vicar general acts within the authority granted by universal and particular law and by the diocesan bishop. The office is diocesan and juridical, not a sacramental degree.
A seminarian is not yet a priest and, under current law, is not a cleric merely by entering seminary. Formation includes human, spiritual, intellectual and pastoral dimensions.
The sacristan’s office is practical and liturgical. It does not itself imply ordination, although clergy or religious may serve as sacristans in particular institutions.
A friar can be a priest or a non-ordained brother. The term describes a religious-family tradition, not a sacramental rank.
A diocese is an ecclesial jurisdiction, not merely a geographic area or administrative brand. Its bishop, clergy, parishes and faithful form the particular Church according to canon law.
The scope of an episcopal vicar is defined by appointment and law. The title does not mean he is himself necessarily a bishop.
A parochial vicar works under the pastor according to law and the bishop’s arrangements. In French this office is commonly called vicaire paroissial.
A rector of a church has defined rights and duties concerning worship and pastoral activity there. The office should not be confused with a seminary rector or a generic administrative director.
A chaplain’s competence is defined by appointment and law. The term can cover hospitals, schools, military or religious communities and other groups, so context matters.
The vicar forane or dean assists diocesan coordination but does not become the proper pastor of every parish in the deanery.
A provincial’s authority is real but limited to the province and powers granted by universal and proper law. The office is distinct from the supreme moderator of the whole institute.
Monsignor indicates a papal honorific or office-related style, depending on context. It does not make the priest a bishop and should never be treated as a sacramental rank.
The novitiate has legal requirements for admission, duration, place and formation. A novice is not yet a professed religious by reason of novitiate alone.
A priory can be independent or dependent on another house depending on the order. The title alone does not establish the house’s autonomy or canonical rank.
Not every bishop is a diocesan bishop: auxiliaries, titular bishops and bishops holding other offices can possess episcopal orders without governing a diocese as its diocesan bishop.

In English ‘pastor’ here is a canonical office, not a generic synonym for every priest or minister. In French the ordinary canonical equivalent is curé or, according to context, pasteur propre de la paroisse.

A priest can celebrate Mass, absolve sacramentally when he has the required faculty, anoint the sick and exercise other ministries according to law. Priesthood is a sacramental order; offices such as pastor, rector or chaplain are separate juridical assignments.

The deacon is truly ordained but is not a priest. In the traditional Solemn Mass the deacon has specific liturgical functions; these ceremonial roles must be distinguished from the sacramental definition of the diaconate itself.
This sense of canon, canonicus, is entirely distinct from the Canon of the Mass and from a canon as an individual legal norm.
Provost is not one universal canonical office with identical powers everywhere. The governing statutes and historical context determine its meaning.
An abbess exercises the authority granted by canon law and the institute’s constitutions within the religious community. She does not receive Holy Orders by reason of that office.
The Eucharist is both sacrament and sacrifice in the Church’s life. After consecration Christ is present whole and entire under each species and under each part of either species when divided.
The Real Presence is not a merely symbolic, subjective or temporary presence dependent on the communicant’s faith. It begins at consecration and endures while the Eucharistic species remain.
Sacramentals are distinct from the seven sacraments. Blessings, blessed objects and certain rites can be sacramentals; their efficacy is not the sacramental efficacy described by ex opere operato.
Baptism remits original sin and all personal sins, gives sanctifying grace and imprints an indelible sacramental character. It is the gateway to the other sacraments.
Viaticum is the Eucharist received in view of death and is distinct from Anointing or Extreme Unction, though these sacraments may be received in the same period of serious illness.
Sacred Chrism is solemnly consecrated by a bishop and has a distinctive sacramental and liturgical use. In the traditional Roman Pontifical its consecration belongs to the rites of the holy oils.

The Catholic Church recognizes seven sacraments. They are efficacious signs of grace, not merely reminders of faith; their fruit in the recipient also depends on the dispositions required by the sacrament.

The faithful are bound to confess mortal sins according to the Church’s requirements; venial sins may also be confessed and this practice is commended. Sacramental confession must not be confused with the broader Latin verb confiteri, which can mean confess, acknowledge or profess.

In the Roman tradition the principal holy oils are the Oil of the Sick, the Oil of Catechumens and Sacred Chrism. They have distinct rites and uses and should not be treated as interchangeable substances.

Confirmation is truly a sacrament and imprints an indelible character. Its Roman ceremonies and disciplinary details can differ between the traditional and current liturgical books without changing the sacrament’s identity.

Holy Communion is not simply attendance at Mass or spiritual union in a broad sense. It is the actual reception of the consecrated Eucharistic species according to the Church’s sacramental discipline.

The Council of Trent calls this conversion fittingly and properly transubstantiation. The term protects the claim that the change is objective and substantial, not merely a change of use, meaning or perception.

Penance reconciles the baptized sinner with God and the Church. Contrition, confession and satisfaction are acts of the penitent; absolution is the sacramental act of the priest exercising the power of the keys.

Absolution is not merely a declaration that the penitent has forgiven himself or already stands forgiven independently of the sacrament. Valid absolution requires a validly ordained priest with the faculty or jurisdiction required by the Church, subject to the law governing particular cases.

Trent teaches Extreme Unction as a true sacrament instituted by Christ. The older Roman books employ the title and a fuller series of anointings; current Roman discipline commonly uses the title Anointing of the Sick. The glossary keeps the layers distinct.
The Roman stational tradition links appointed churches with particular liturgical days. ‘Station’ here must be distinguished from an individual Station of the Cross.

The apostolate is not reserved to clergy. Lay Catholics have real responsibilities in their families, professions and associations, while ecclesial authority, sacramental ministry and teaching offices retain their proper distinctions.
Pilgrim describes the devotional role of the traveler and does not itself imply membership in an association, fulfilment of a vow or participation in an officially organized event.
Historical confraternities had varying canonical forms, privileges and obligations. A modern directory should not infer current canonical standing merely from an old confraternity title.
Sodality is a broad historical term rather than one single current canonical form. The precise juridical status of a given sodality must be established from its statutes and competent authority.
